title: Ishak of Mosul and His Mistress and the Devil

full_text:
Ishak of Mosul, the illustrious court musician of Harun al-Rashid, was challenged one evening at the palace of Prince Ibrahim to an artistic contest by an anonymous traveling lutenist from Andalusia.

The Andalusian musician played with breathtaking speed, introducing novel syncopated rhythms and intricate finger-plucking techniques that left the court spellbound.

Ishak, who had never encountered such western rhythms, at first felt an itch of artistic envy; but being a true master of noble character, he suppressed the unworthy emotion.

Instead of disputing the foreigner’s skill, Ishak took his own lute, absorbed the new rhythms into his mind, and wove them into the ancient classical modes of Baghdad, creating a musical synthesis of such sublime beauty, emotional power, and technical brilliance that the entire assembly—including the Andalusian—stood and cheered with boundless delight!

The Andalusian master embraced Ishak before the Caliph: 'I came from the shores of Cordoba thinking to humble the master of Baghdad; but I have found that true genius does not fight its rivals; it embraces new beauty and elevates the art of all humankind!'

Harun al-Rashid rewarded both masters with robes of honor, and Ishak incorporated the Andalusian modes into the musical curriculum of Baghdad, proving that art flourishes through generous exchange rather than petty rivalry.
moral: Artistic competition should inspire creative elevation, not bitter jealousy.
